newsitem.title: USA: FDA advisory panel rejects Gehrig's disease drug.
newsitem.headline: FDA advisory panel rejects Gehrig's disease drug.

text.p: A panel of Food and Drug Administration advisers Thursday voted to reject a new drug for the treatment of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), or Lou Gehrig's disease, which kills 10,000 Americans a year and affects up to 30,000.
In a 6-3 decision, the panel voted against recommending approval of Cephalon Inc.'s Myotrophin (recombinant human insulin growth factor-1) injection for ALS.
Cephalon and its partner, Chiron Corp., had struggled to win FDA approval. The agency is not bound by the panel's advice, but usually follows it.
ALS causes progressive paralysis and loss of respiratory function. Patients survive only about three years after diagnosis.

More than 20 ALS sufferers, some of whom were in wheelchairs and spoke with great difficulty, pleaded tearfully and passionately for approval of Myotrophin, saying that it would give them hope and time.
But panel chairman Dr. Sid Gilman, of the University of Michigan Medical Center, said that "the data do not look robust, they look modest."

Dr. David Drachman, a panelist from the University of Massachusetts, said, "my sense is we have seen cosmetic changes in the data," adding that the panel was exactly where it was last June --- wanting better and more information.
Almost a year ago, the same advisory committee reviewed Cephalon's request to expand access to the drug on an experimental basis.

Cephalon subsequently won that clearance based on early results of a North American and a European study, but the panel wanted the company to conduct an additional full-blown trial to buttress what it called weak data. Cephalon instead reanalyzed the two trials and did some smaller supporting studies.
"We are deeply disappointed with the committee's finding," Cephalon President and Chief Executive Officer, Dr. William Rutter, said in a statement.

Wall Street analysts said they expected the news would cause the stock prices of both Cephalon and Emeryville, Calif.-based Chiron to drop on Friday. Myotrophin was the lead drug candidate for Westchester, Pa.-based Cephalon, a development stage biotechnology company that has not yet brought any products to market.

"They're both going down and Cephalon is going to go down substantially," Mehta and Isaly analyst Carl Gordon, said of the companies' share prices. "I think the expectations had been fairly favorable. People thought they had a shot (at approval)."
Shares of Cephalon and, to a lesser extent, Chiron, had been volatile since last June, when Myotrophin first went before the FDA advisory panel.

A drug for ALS is already on the market -- Rhone-Poulenc Rorer's Rilutek (riluzole) -- which was approved by the FDA in December, 1995. The disease gets its common name from the Yankee baseball great Lou Gehrig, who died of it. It attacks nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord.
